title: Training urged to keep alcoholics safe in custody
article: A coroner's jury probing the death of a 45-year-old Dunnville man has recommended specialized training for police officers and prison guards in recognizing the signs and dangers of chronic alcohol withdrawal.
Wallace Little, who drank up to 36 bottles of beer a day, died at the Haldimand War Memorial Hospital in Dunnville on June 2, 2005, after he was arrested by Cayuga OPP following a domestic dispute.

After spending the night in police custody, he first started showing symptoms of alcohol withdrawal when he appeared for a bail hearing before a justice of the peace in Cayuga the following morning. When the JP noticed he had the shakes, he ordered police to take him to the hospital for treatment.
During the inquest before coroner Dr. Jack Stanborough this week, the jury heard Little died of "acute alcohol withdrawal syndrome" about four hours after he was taken to the hospital.
The jurors also heard police had treated him compassionately while he was in custody and that Little had insisted he was OK when police asked him if he needed help.

During the inquest, Little's family doctor testified the deceased was a chronic alcoholic and the doctor had warned his family shortly before his arrest that it was only a matter of time before he succumbed to the disease.

Dr. Graeme Cunningham, an expert in alcohol withdrawal syndrome, testified about the risks that chronic alcoholics face in custody when their alcohol supply is suddenly cut off. He suggested guards and police should wait until an inmate sobers up before trying to determine whether they are a chronic alcoholic. They should then ask two key questions: Have you ever had seizures from drinking? Have you ever experienced DTs (delirium tremens)?

As part of their recommendations, the jurors said the Ontario Police College and the OPP College should use the Little case as a scenario in teaching guards and police about the dangers of alcohol withdraw syndrome.

The jurors also recommended that the officer in charge of a unit should document any medical or mental health issues on the inmate's arrest sheet and record any self-disclosed alcohol or drug abuse, regardless of whether symptoms are shown at time of arrest.
The jurors said police agencies may also consider including a section in their policy manual describing the signs of alcohol withdrawal.
